Facebook Twitter Print Email From drought to deluge: ‘Super’ El Niño’s expanding reach 6 October 2026 Climate and Environment Across Papua New Guinea, water sources are drying up, crops are failing and food prices are rising months before the worst agricultural impacts are expected. Behind those warning signs is an El Niño whose Pacific Ocean temperatures have already surpassed the equivalent measurements during the historic 1997 and 2015 events – part of an unfolding climate pattern being dubbed a “Super El Niño” by some climate watchers. Fast facts More than 347 million children in nearly 100 countries and territories are expected to experience unusually wet or dry conditions between October and December 2026 due to El Niño, increasing the risk of extreme floods and droughts with potentially devastating consequences, according to latest UNICEF data. Here are highlights of the risks facing children: As extreme weather events become more widespread, youngsters could face increased risks of family separation, violence, exploitation and child marriage Colombia, Fiji, Papua New Guinea and the Philippines are among those expected to experience drier conditions that could likely to lead to drought and water scarcity, increasing displacement and worsening acute malnutrition In the Greater Horn of Africa , wetter-than-normal conditions could trigger flash flooding, spread water-borne diseases and disrupt schooling In crisis and conflict-affected countries such as Afghanistan and Chad , El Niño can be a direct threat to survival, worsening hunger and malnutrition among already vulnerable children Every $1 invested in disaster risk reduction and prevention can save up to $15 in recovery costs, yet less than one per cent of humanitarian funding currently goes to anticipatory action The 2026-2027 El Niño is forecast to become one of the strongest on record, threatening to intensify drought, floods and other weather extremes across countries already grappling with food insecurity, displacement and economic pressures. Children on the frontlines, again El Niño can shift rainfall patterns thousands of kilometres from the tropical Pacific, leaving some regions facing drought and water shortages while others contend with heavier rains, flooding and heightened disease risks. More than 347 million children in nearly 100 countries and territories could be exposed to unusually dry or wet conditions between October and December because of El Niño, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) warns in a new analysis . “For children, El Niño is far more than a weather pattern. It can mean increased displacement, malnutrition, water shortages and disease outbreaks,” said UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell. “Children are also at risk of schools closing, while families could experience added financial hardship.” Already, 1.1 billion children – nearly half of the world’s children – are already exposed to at least three overlapping climate-related hazards such as drought, extreme heat or floods. In Papua New Guinea, impact is already here Some of those consequences are already visible in Papua New Guinea, a mountainous Pacific island nation where remote terrain and difficult logistics have complicated responses to previous droughts. El Niño conditions have been present since mid-2026 and are forecast to peak between October and December. In September, the Niño 3.4 index – a measure of sea surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific used to track El Niño – surpassed those recorded during every previous El Niño event, including 1997 and 2015. The Government, which declared the event in June, has established a dedicated task force and approved a $112 million supplementary budget. Yet, needs are mounting. Some 1.2 million people are estimated to require direct food relief, with water shortages, crop losses, dwindling food reserves and higher prices already reported. Schools are being disrupted and concerns are growing over health, nutrition and bushfires. The largest impacts on agriculture and food security are expected from November. One ocean, very different extremes What dries out one part of the world can bring deluges to another. Across the Greater Horn of Africa, wetter-than-normal conditions could raise the risk of river and flash flooding, increase the spread of waterborne diseases and disrupt schooling. In the wider region – including Yemen, Sudan and Afghanistan – children living amid conflict and displacement face particularly acute risks because El Niño can magnify existing hunger, malnutrition and difficulties accessing essential services.
